translations.text: By Saint John Chrysostom. A discourse on fasting and on Joseph.
And on the priest and on David. Blessed David went among us all in turn, singing a song in sections.
I will confess to you, Lord, with all my heart; I will tell of all your wonders.
Oh, what very great doubt concerning blessed David, who sinned
and neglected himself! For although, as a human being, he stumbled and fell, nevertheless,
as a human being he confessed. I will confess to you, Lord, with all my heart.
For if I do not confess to you, I will not escape my sins. I will confess to you, Lord, with all my heart. For if I
do not confess to you, I will not become white as snow. I will confess to you, Lord, with all my heart.
For if I do not confess to you, the deceitful devil, mocking me for murder and adultery,
will not leave me alone. I will confess to you, Lord, with all my heart.
For if I do not confess to you, I will not rise to my former honor.
I will confess to you, Lord, with all my heart. For if I do not confess to you,
I cannot be called a son in the flesh. I will confess to you, Lord, with all my heart.
For if I do not confess to you, the Holy Spirit says nothing to me.
No one, then, can learn the fiftieth psalm. It is fitting for each of those who come
to holy baptism to speak the words of blessed David.
10. I will confess to you, Lord, with all my heart. For if I do not confess to you,
I will not put off the old self. I will confess to you, Lord, with all my heart.
For if I do not confess to you, I will not put on the new self.
I will confess to you, Lord, with all my heart. For if I do not confess to you,
I will not join the flock of the faithful. I will confess to you, Lord, with all my heart. For I have heard you say:
Do not be ashamed to confess your sins. I will confess to you, Lord, with all my heart.
For I have heard you say clearly: I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.
Now it is time to bring forward the sayings of blessed Paul as well. Which ones? Those in which he said: Now is the acceptable time.
What time? The adornment of fasting. What time? The radiance of love for the poor.
What time [?] the harvest of repentance. Now is the acceptable time; now is the time of salvation.
The Preacher himself writes and says: “A time to weep and a time to laugh.” Listen carefully.
Holy Scripture says nothing without meaning, but is entirely filled with the Spirit of God.
A time to weep and a time to bow down. A time to weep over sin and a time to laugh over salvation.
To laugh, but not to mock. For laughter that ridicules is one thing, and laughter that benefits is another. And to show that I am not lying,
learn this, and take instruction from Holy Scripture about mocking laughter too.
Listen to Solomon, who says in his wisdom: “Doing evil is laughter to a fool.”
But concerning good and beneficial laughter,
listen to James, who says: “He will not accept any gift from the ungodly.”
“But truthful lips will not have their fill of laughter.” So the Preacher spoke well:
“A time to weep and a time to laugh.” A time to weep over sin, and a time to love righteousness.
For the Lord is righteous and loves righteousness. For there is a time to cast away enmity,
and, in turn, not to neglect love. But let us listen to blessed Paul, who says:
“Do not let the sun set on your anger.” A time to uproot ungodliness,
and a time to plant godliness. For our Lord himself, writing to the prophet Jeremiah
about the Jewish lands overgrown with thorns, said to him: “See, today I appoint you to dig out roots
and to plant again, to tear down and to build again.” To uproot the worship of many gods,
and to plant one sovereign rule. To uproot and to build. To uproot the pagan places of sacrifice,
and to build churches of the martyrs. “See, today I appoint you.”
Do not understand this as referring to a fixed day, but to all times and always. As Saint Paul said:
“Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion.”
That is, on whatever day you hear the Lord saying, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near,”
do not harden your hearts by pretending to be pure.
These things apply not only before baptism and under the Law, but also after the baptism of grace.
For the Master himself, Christ, said in other words, as he gave instruction to his disciples:
Truly I tell you: whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven. And this is not merely a matter of words.
Rather, he also empowered his disciples through deeds to loose and to bind. Look first of all at blessed Peter:
how he bound with death Ananias and Sapphira, who had conspired to lie;
and how he released from his bonds the man who had been lame from birth, strengthening his feet that very moment.
What will those who pretend to be pure say to this—[?] those purer than themselves?
Yet they themselves are the most unclean of all. For no one is pure, even if he lives on earth for only one day.
What will those who dare to speak with their foolish mouths say against this:
“Must I come to this priest and confess my sins
when he has sinned many times more than I have? How can such a sinful man wipe away sins?”
But it is good, in a time of hunger, to set before you the remedies of repentance for your follies, O man.
Do you think that you are coming to a human being, or that a human being forgives your sins?
You come to the Lord God through an intercessor, for the forgiveness of your sins. Your mediator and master
before God is the priest. Why, then, do you condemn someone whom God does not condemn? As long as he is a priest
and God grants him the priesthood, do not refuse to receive God's holiness from him.
For it is not he who grants you forgiveness of sins, but the Ruler who gave him the priesthood, acting through an intercessor.
And just as, not only under grace but also before grace, the God of all has always brought salvation to people
through a human being, for this reason our Lord became human, a mediator between God and human beings.
You yourselves, being very fond of learning, know the account of blessed David,
who has just proclaimed: “I will confess to you, O Lord, with all my heart.”
How David, having fallen into murder and adultery, remained in evil without confessing. What, then, did God do
to bring him too to repentance? He also provided examples of repentance, so that he would accept repentance.
He sent Nathan the prophet to him, presenting the matter as though it concerned someone else and concealing that it concerned him.
For the prophet just mentioned came to David and said, “O king, I have something to tell you.”
David said, “Speak quickly.” Then Nathan the prophet said, “There was a certain rich man who had livestock and many herds.
There was also a poor man who had one heifer, which ate with him at his table.”
And she drank from the same cup with him and slept in his arms.
He calls David the rich man and Uriah the poor man. What, then, did Nathan say? “A stranger [?] to the rich man.”
For the rich man, sparing his own herds, sent and took the poor man’s heifer and slaughtered her for the stranger.
Although King David had fallen into sin, he was nevertheless shown to be righteous:
on the one hand through bodily sin, and on the other through the correction of his soul.
For he answered angrily and said, “As the Lord lives, such a man deserves death!
And he must repay the heifer sevenfold.” David goes beyond the law: the law prescribed fourfold repayment.
And what did Nathan say to David? “You, O king, are the one who did this.” Then David, being wise and living with understanding,
did not exalt himself because of his royal dignity. He did not torture him or say, “Who is this
who has dared to proclaim so great an insult against me before everyone?”
For he knew clearly that, although he was a king, he was under the authority of a King
over whom no king has power. As soon as David heard this,
he immediately answered, “I have sinned against the Lord.” And Nathan immediately said there,
“The Lord has forgiven your sin; you will not die.” O Nathan, on what grounds do you dare
to wish to answer, when challenged by Novatus? David sinned against God, and to him
he confessed. How do you know whether he has forgiven him or not? Learn first, and then teach.
And Nathan said, “God entrusted David’s twofold path to me.”
Who will reproach a physician who labors and undertakes so long a journey? He will clearly show
that God has given people salvation not only under grace, but also before grace.
Let us also take a brief account to make clear what is being said. Tell me, O man,
you who make yourself an opponent of repentance. Tell me of a man who has sinned
and has been thrown into prison, into prison, by a ruler,
when the ruler wishes either to send him away somewhere or to hand him over to some torture.
Do you think he comes to the ruler himself and begs to escape his trouble? Will he not seek an intercessor for himself,
even, to speak plainly, someone inferior to himself, so that through someone he might at least escape his suffering?
Is there order in bodily matters, but lawlessness in spiritual matters?
But, O man, if you refuse to come to repentance because the priest is a sinful human being,
then do not be baptized either, for the one who baptizes you is a human being. Nor should you receive Holy Communion,
for the one who breaks it is a human being. But if you trust him because he has faith,
then receive this too with faith. For the one who baptizes and offers
the spotless sacrifice does nothing else but raise his hands to the holy and pure Trinity.
Likewise, the one who prescribes repentance for you does nothing else but bring about your salvation with his tongue.
But the opponents will immediately say, “If this is so—”
And, unwilling to accept salvation through repentance after baptism: “Why did blessed Peter put Ananias and Sapphira to death there at once,
instead of turning them back through repentance?” For this is what some people say. But listen carefully.
Blessed Peter did not conceal the healing of repentance. Rather, Ananias and Sapphira, who fell into such great trouble,
were unwilling to seek the readily available healing of repentance, but perished through the devil’s prompting,
and with the word and their property [?]. For repentance is genuine when it is not honored merely in speech,
but when it is recognized by deeds. For there is repentance brought forth from the whole soul,
and there is repentance sought merely among the citizens. Through it some are saved,
while others are condemned. Blessed Peter repented, and so did wicked Judas.
But Peter repented properly, wept, and washed away his denial with tears,
and entered once more into the radiance of his former faith. Judas, however, neglected repentance,
although he threw the silver down before the Jews and said to them, “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood.”
Nevertheless, he did not rise up or weep, nor did he do anything that belonged to good repentance, but only wove a noose for the devil
and made himself known [?]. But the opponents will immediately say—for I cannot refrain from recounting their
wicked arguments—“What, then, about Simon the magician, who was baptized, became angry, and was condemned by Peter?
He brought gifts to buy the gift that cannot be sold. He asked for repentance. Did not blessed Peter answer him,
saying, ‘Repent of this wickedness and pray to the Lord’? Why, then, did he not say to Ananias and Sapphira
these same words: ‘Repent of your wickedness’?” Such are their arguments. But listen with understanding.
The gift of the Holy One is not to be mocked. For Ananias and Sapphira, when rebuked by blessed Peter,
and hearing him say, “Why did you agree together to put the Spirit of the Lord to the test?”
did not confess their sin, did not fall down or plead, and did not say, “We have sinned as human beings do.”
Instead, when rebuked by Peter, they opposed his words, thinking they could hide from him,
and not understanding that there is no way to mock the Holy Spirit.
Therefore blessed Peter immediately became angry at this and gave them the answer they deserved.
But Simon heard blessed Peter say, “May your silver perish with you, because you thought that God's gift could be acquired in exchange
for possessions.” When he heard this, he did not become angry, did not feel sorry for himself, and did not withdraw.
Instead, he accepted the reproaches and insults as good remedies,
and, falling down before not only Peter but all the apostles, he said, “Pray to the Lord for me,
so that none of the things you have announced may come upon me. I have sinned greatly.
I do not dare to pray to God on my own. Pray for me yourselves. Be my intercessors; offer a prayer for me.”
So Ecclesiastes rightly says, “A time to weep and a time to bow down,” for those who love repentance.
For in this way the great Joseph also wept, looking ahead with a prophet's eye,
joining blessed David, who says, “Those who sow in tears will reap in joy.”
Joseph sowed tears of brotherly love and reaped the crown of kingship.
For you all plainly know of that wondrous recognition, when Joseph saw his brothers,
whom he did not wish to call brothers. For what kind of brothers were they to him, who, from a braid of twelve strands,
tore one strand away from themselves? Yet Joseph turned his great sorrow into mercy and fell upon his brothers' necks.
He wept over them. Why upon their necks and not elsewhere? It was fitting that he wept upon the necks of those
who had thrown off the yoke of brotherhood. Do you see the man's gentleness and self-control?
But some will say of Joseph that he was beset by hardship,
and was in a foreign land, with no human help or protection, and that this was why he had gentleness
and humility. But listen carefully, you who say such things: you speak with a wealth of words,
but not with truth. For Joseph himself, through his goodness and self-control,
He was clothed in his father's goodness. They remembered Joseph, and that light came [?]. For Christ, the Lord of light,
released him from the darkness of prison. Yet you speak at length without understanding, O man,
and not truthfully, saying that Joseph was good and innocent by compulsion.
Such was Joseph, a lover of God, who was a law before the Law existed. Even when he was enticed and pressured
by the Egyptian woman, he abhorred and fled the act of adultery.
Do you suppose a law had been given, commanding people not to commit adultery, murder, steal, or bear false witness?
But he was a law to himself, and, taught by his natural judgment, he fled naked,
so that he would not defile his master's place. Did not his mistress plead with him earnestly, promising him freedom,
if only he would obey her and give her pleasure? But the more she pursued him,
the more he avoided her, making himself a eunuch according to the Lord's word,
not with a knife, but through faith. Did not Joseph address the Egyptian woman with these words, saying:
“Since my master, madam, because of me, does not concern himself with anything he has in the house,
but has put everything into my hands, and concerns himself with nothing except you, because you are his wife,
how can I do this devilish deed and sin before God?
Do you say that the God of my fathers is not here? Do you say that there is one God in the land of Canaan
and another in Egypt, even if you do not understand? Do you say that God's all-seeing power is not here,
watching everything? If your husband is outside, madam, has my God gone away with him?
Your husband, madam, is my master, and he has entrusted all his possessions to my hands.
How can I dishonor his rib? God has joined one man to one woman,
not one woman to many men, nor many women to one man. Be silent, then, madam.
I know who sets you aflame against me. It is not you who torment me, madam, but the one who stirred up my brothers against me.
He is the devil. Having already deprived me of my father, he strives to separate me from God as well.
He turns this way and that, trying to deprive me of the dream I saw.
Be silent, then, madam. Be content to bear the name of adulteress without committing the act. If I obey you,
my body suffers harm. But if I disobey God, I suffer torment in both ways.”
For he knew the one who was going to say, “Fear the one who can destroy both soul and body
in eternal fire.” Such is the account of the gentleness of steadfast Joseph.
But listen also to these deeds of his. For you all know well
that he was thrown into prison because of his mistress’s accusations.
Then, when the appointed time had ended—or rather, when the revelation [?] was coming to fulfillment—
and his brothers had come to Egypt because of the famine, Joseph saw them.
Though he was king and ruled over all Egypt, he did not draw his sword, shut them in prison, starve them to death, or inflict wounds on them.
Nor did he plot against them as against beasts, though beasts they were. He did not recall the tearing of his coat or the depths of the pit,
or the sufferings of slavery, or the envy of his kin, or the hateful smoke of brotherly love,
or being deprived of his father [?], or the suffering of his own brother Benjamin.
Instead, putting all this beneath his feet and mixing threats with [?], he sought an occasion to make himself known to his brothers.
As soon as he saw his brothers and his own brother Benjamin,
the innocent young one, the youngest, the last cluster on his father’s vine, untouched by his brothers’ lack of love,
a brother both by nature and in mind, he immediately wept for joy and, turning, cried out,
saying, “I am Joseph. But now do not let this seem harsh to you.” Oh, what a marvelous deed!
The innocent man answers as though guilty: “I am Joseph, your brother.
If you had bowed down unwillingly, my dream would have been a lie, and my sheaf would not have stood upright.
You would rightly have sharpened your grief with hatred for your brother. At least learn this, brothers:
everyone who trusts in the Lord will not be put to shame. You stripped me of a plain coat;
look, I sit clothed in purple. You threw me into a pit; look, I sit in a chariot plated with gold.
You sold me as a slave; look, I am a king. I was in prison; look, I live with royal authority. I was in chains;
look, I wear a royal crown of precious stones.” It is fitting, then, brothers, for us to proclaim the words of blessed Paul:
“All things work together for good for those who love God.” To him be glory, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
